The '''Quinnipiac University Poll''' is a [[public opinion polling]] center based at [[Quinnipiac University]] in [[Hamden, Connecticut]]. It surveys public opinion in [[Connecticut]], [[Florida]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], [[Iowa]], [[Michigan]], [[Minnesota]], [[New York (state)|New York]], [[New Jersey]], [[North Carolina]], [[Pennsylvania]], [[Ohio]], [[Texas]], [[Virginia]], [[Wisconsin]] and nationally.<ref name=mission>{{Cite web|title=Quinnipiac University/Poll: Polls |work=quinnipiac.edu |publisher=[[Quinnipiac University]] |url=https://poll.qu.edu/poll-results/}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Silver |first=Nate |date=2021-03-25 |title=Pollster Ratings - Quinnipiac University |url=https://projects.fivethirtyeight.com/pollster-ratings/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141005201227/http://projects.fivethirtyeight.com/pollster-ratings/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=October 5, 2014 |access-date=2022-03-22 |website=FiveThirtyEight |language=en}}</ref> The poll is unaffiliated with any academic department at the school and is run by Quinnipiac's public relations department.<ref name=":1" />  

Academic-affiliated polls like Quinnipiac have grown in significance as media budgets have declined, and in 2017 [[Politico]] called the Quinnipiac poll "the most significant player among a number of schools that have established a national polling footprint."<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Shepard |first=Steven |date=2017-12-12 |title=The Poll That Built a University |url=http://politi.co/2BVyU4y |access-date=2022-06-01 |website=POLITICO Magazine |language=en}}</ref> 

It is considerably larger than other academic polling centers, including the [[Franklin & Marshall College Poll]], which only surveys Pennsylvania.<ref name=lieberman>{{Cite news | last = Lieberman| first = Brett| title = Behind the scenes at the Q-Poll| newspaper = [[Patriot-News]]| date = April 9, 2007| url = http://blog.pennlive.com/pennsyltucky/2007/04/behind_the_scenes_at_the_qpoll.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111001074901/http://blog.pennlive.com/pennsyltucky/2007/04/behind_the_scenes_at_the_qpoll.html| url-status = live|archive-date=October 1, 2011}}</ref> The organization employs about 300 interviewers, generally drawing about a quarter of its employees from [[political science]], [[communications]], [[psychology]], and [[sociology]] majors, and the remainder of interviewers from those not affiliated with the university.<ref name=lieberman /> The poll has a full-time staff of ten.<ref name=lieberman />  The university does not disclose Quinnipiac University Poll's operating budget, and the poll does not accept clients or outside funding.<ref name=lieberman />

== History ==
The polling operation began informally in 1988 in conjunction with a marketing class.<ref name="slate101608"/>  It became formal in 1996 when the university hired a [[CBS News]] analyst to assess the data being gained.<ref name="slate101608"/>  It subsequently focused on the Northeastern states, gradually expanding during presidential elections to cover [[swing state]]s as well.<ref name="slate101608"/>  The institute is funded by the university.<ref name="slate101608"/> Quinnipiac University is widely known for its poll;<ref name="nyt122607">{{cite news | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/12/26/sports/ncaabasketball/26quinnipiac.html | title=New Quinnipiac Coach Is Expected to Build a Winner | author=Weinreb, Michael | newspaper=[[The New York Times]] | date=December 26, 2007 | access-date=April 24, 2009}}</ref> the publicity it has generated has been credited with increasing the university's enrollment.<ref name=lieberman />

In 2007, Quinnipiac University Poll underwent construction of a new two-story building that was expected to double its available capacity to 160 calling cubicles.<ref name=lieberman /> The purpose of the capacity expansion was to allow polling multiple states at once, rectifying a problem that arose during the [[United States Senate election in Connecticut, 2006|2006 Connecticut Senate election]] where other polls were canceled to support that poll.<ref name=lieberman />

The poll has been cited by major news outlets throughout North America and Europe, including ''[[The Washington Post]]'',<ref>{{Cite news | last = LaCruz| first = Donna| title = Polls: Menendez Leads Kean in N.J. Race | newspaper = [[Washington Post]]| date = October 31, 2006| url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2006/10/31/AR2006103100231.html}}</ref> [[Fox News]],<ref>{{Cite news | title = Poll: Lieberman Leads Challenger Lamont in Connecticut Senate Race | newspaper = [[Fox News Channel]] | date = August 17, 2006| url = https://www.foxnews.com/story/poll-lieberman-leads-challenger-lamont-in-connecticut-senate-race}}</ref> ''[[USA Today]]'',<ref>{{Cite news | title = Quinnipiac Poll: Giuliani still leads GOP hopefuls, but by much less | newspaper = [[USA Today]]| date = May 21, 2010| url = http://blogs.usatoday.com/onpolitics/2007/05/giuliani_still_.html | archive-url = https://archive.today/20070625054541/http://blogs.usatoday.com/onpolitics/2007/05/giuliani_still_.html | archive-date = June 25, 2007 | access-date=May 22, 2010 | url-status=dead}}</ref> ''[[The New York Times]]'',<ref>{{Cite news | last = Kapochunas| first = Rachel | title = Poll Tests ‘New York-New York-New York’ Race in Ohio
| newspaper = [[New York Times]]| date = July 13, 2007| url = https://www.nytimes.com/cq/2007/07/13/cq_3078.html}}</ref> [[CNN]],<ref>{{cite news| url=http://www.cnn.com/2012/03/13/justice/new-york-police-muslims-poll/index.html | work=CNN | title= Poll: Majority of New Yorkers approve of NYPD surveillance of Muslims|last=Boyette|first=Chris}}</ref> and [[Reuters]].<ref>{{Cite news | last = Sullivan | first = Andy | title = Obama leads in four battleground states: poll | newspaper = [[Reuters]]| date = Jun 26, 2008 | url = https://www.reuters.com/article/topNews/idUSN2631671720080626}}</ref> Quinnipiac University Poll receives national recognition for its independent surveys of residents throughout the United States. It conducts public opinion polls on politics and public policy as a public service as well as for academic research.<ref name=lieberman /><ref name="slate101608">{{cite magazine|url=http://www.slate.com/id/2202433/|title=What's With All the "Quinnipiac University" Polls? How an obscure school in Connecticut turned into a major opinion research center.|first=Juliet|last=Lapidos|magazine=Slate|date=October 16, 2008}}</ref> Poll results are also aggregated by [[ABC News (United States)|ABC News]]' [[FiveThirtyEight]].<ref name=":0" /> [[Andrew S. Tanenbaum]], the founder of the poll-analysis website [[Electoral-vote.com]], compared major pollsters' performances in the [[United States Senate elections, 2010|2010 midterm Senate elections]] and concluded that Quinnipiac was the most accurate, with a mean error of 2.0 percent.<ref>{{Cite web| last = Tanenbaum  | first = Andrew S.| author-link = Andrew S. Tanenbaum| title = Analysis of the Pollsters | publisher = [[Electoral-vote.com]]| date = November 9, 2010| url = http://www.electoral-vote.com/evp2010/Senate/Maps/Nov09-s.html#1| access-date = 2011-01-24}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/rasmussen-polls-were-biased-and-inaccurate-quinnipiac-surveyusa-performed-strongly/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140323223941/http://fivethirtyeight.com/features/rasmussen-polls-were-biased-and-inaccurate-quinnipiac-surveyusa-performed-strongly/|url-status=dead|archive-date=March 23, 2014|title=Rasmussen Polls Were Biased and Inaccurate; Quinnipiac, SurveyUSA Performed Strongly|date=5 November 2010|work=[[FiveThirtyEight]]|access-date=25 March 2017}}</ref>

Politico reported in 2018 that "much of Quinnipiac’s prominence in the field is also a result of its commitment to self-promotion." The publication pointed out that the poll "reports to the university’s public-affairs office, not any academic wing of the school," and that for many years the poll employed New York publicist [[Howard J. Rubenstein|Howard Rubenstein]] and prominent journalists to promote the poll.<ref name=":1" />

== Methodology ==
The Quinnipiac University Poll conducts polling through [[random digit dialing]] with live interviewers. Polls utilize 100-200 interviewers consisting of university students and Hamden residents, dialing both landlines and cell phones. Phone numbers are obtained from market research company [[Dynata]]. In the event of a missed call, Quinnipiac attempts four call-backs. If a household with multiple members is reached, interviewers ask to speak to the individual with the closest upcoming birthday as a quasirandom within-household selection method. Polls are typically conducted over a five-day period and aim to gather a random sample of about 1,500 respondents.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ctinsider.com/politics/article/ct-quinnipiac-poll-methods-fivethirtyeight-2024-18648792.php|title=While other pollsters pivot online, the CT-based Quinnipiac Poll is standing by its phones in 2024|date=February 18, 2024|work=CT Insider}}</ref><ref name = QUmethod>{{cite web|url=https://poll.qu.edu/methodology/|title=Methodology|access-date = 29 September 2024|work=Quinnipiac}}</ref> 

Responses to polls are weighted with [[US Census]] demographic data, adjusting for the variables of age, education, gender, race, and region.<ref name = "QUmethod"/>

Quinnipiac University polls target American adults aged 18 and over. For political polling, Quinnipiac identifies registered and likely voters from screening questions. The poll emphasizes results from surveys of likely voters when approaching election days.<ref name = "QUmethod"/>
